items.text: Have your blood pressure checked in a clinic at least once a year.
items.why: Regular checks find high blood pressure before it causes harm.

items.text: Eat a DASH-style diet and reduce salt added to meals.
items.why: Less salt helps keep blood pressure in a healthy range.

items.text: Keep a healthy weight and a waist-to-height ratio below 0.5.
items.why: A healthy body size lowers long-term strain on your heart.

items.text: Do 30 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise on 5 to 7 days a week.
items.why: Regular activity supports blood flow and heart fitness.

items.text: Limit alcohol to 2 standard drinks a day for men, or 1.5 for women.
items.why: Too much alcohol raises blood pressure.

items.text: Reduce daily stress and get 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night.
items.why: Good sleep and less stress support healthy blood vessels.

items.text: Get urgent care now for chest pain, severe breathlessness, or blood pressure of 180/110 or higher with headache, chest pain, or blurred vision.
items.why: These can be signs of a heart or blood pressure emergency.

addons.text: Stop smoking completely and ask your healthcare provider about quit support.
addons.why: Quitting protects the lining of your blood vessels.

addons.text: Ask your doctor about getting a lipid profile test.
addons.why: Heart disease in your family makes checking blood fats more important.

addons.text: Avoid processed, canned, and instant foods to lower your salt intake.
addons.why: Processed foods hide a lot of salt.

items.text: Have your fasting blood sugar or HbA1c checked at your yearly health visit.
items.why: Early testing finds blood sugar changes before symptoms appear.

items.text: Choose whole grains, vegetables, and lean proteins, and watch your portion sizes.
items.why: Healthy foods and portions help keep blood sugar steady.

items.text: Drink water instead of sugar-sweetened drinks.
items.why: Fewer sugary drinks lower your daily sugar and calories.

items.why: These can signal a dangerous rise in blood sugar.

items.text: Have your breathing checked at your yearly doctor visit.
items.why: Regular checks find breathing changes early.

items.text: Do not smoke, and stay away from secondhand smoke and e-cigarette vapor.
items.why: Smoke irritates and slowly damages your airways.

items.text: Avoid wood smoke, cooking fumes, dust, and heavy air pollution.
items.why: Breathing in smoke and fumes can inflame your airways.

items.text: Do 30 minutes of moderate activity on at least 5 days a week (150 minutes).
items.why: Regular activity keeps your breathing muscles and stamina strong.

items.text: Ask your doctor whether you should get yearly flu and pneumococcal vaccines.
items.why: Vaccines protect your lungs from serious infections.

items.text: Watch for breathing symptoms such as long-lasting cough, wheezing, or shortness of breath.
items.why: Noticing changes early helps you get advice in time.

items.text: Avoid asthma triggers such as cold air and allergens, and note if you wheeze with exercise or at night.
items.why: Knowing your triggers can point to sensitive airways.

items.text: Get emergency care now for severe breathlessness, trouble speaking in sentences, blue lips, or drowsiness or confusion.
items.why: These are signs of a breathing emergency.

addons.text: Stop smoking completely and ask your healthcare provider about quit programs.
addons.why: Quitting is the most effective way to protect your lungs.

addons.text: Use a proper mask and good ventilation at work.
addons.why: Less exposure prevents lung damage from building up.

addons.trigger: Allergic rhinitis, childhood asthma history, or CRD family history band 3 or 4 (any)
addons.text: Ask your doctor whether you need a lung function test.
addons.why: Nasal allergies, childhood asthma, and lung disease in your family raise your risk.
addons.source: GINA 2026; GOLD 2020, Ch. 1; CDSS Data Dictionary (FHRS)

items.text: If you have thoughts of harming yourself, call the NCMH Crisis Hotline at 1553 or go to the nearest emergency room now.
items.why: Immediate support keeps you safe during a crisis.

items.text: Retake the PHQ-9 (mood) and GAD-7 (anxiety) questionnaires at your yearly check-up.
items.why: Regular tracking shows changes in mood and anxiety over time.

items.text: Do 30 minutes of moderate activity on at least 5 days a week (150 minutes).
items.why: Regular exercise supports a better mood.

items.text: Keep a daily routine and stay connected with family, friends, and others who support you.
items.why: Routines and social contact give emotional stability.

items.text: Keep regular sleep and wake times.
items.why: Good sleep supports emotional health.

items.text: Limit alcohol to 2 standard drinks a day for men, or 1.5 for women.
items.why: Too much alcohol can worsen mood and sleep.

items.text: Get urgent medical care now if you are unable to eat, sleep, or care for yourself.
items.why: Being unable to manage daily needs calls for prompt help.

addons.trigger: Daily sleep below 7 or above 9 hours
addons.text: Aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night with consistent bedtimes.
addons.why: Too little or too much sleep can upset your mood.
addons.source: WHO Module 6; CDSS Data Dictionary (Harrison's, 7 to 9 hours)

addons.text: Cut down or stop drinking alcohol.
addons.why: Alcohol can disturb your mood and sleep.

addons.text: Relax before bed and cut down screen time at bedtime.
addons.why: Better sleep habits improve sleep quality.

addons.trigger: TSH outside 0.34 to 4.25 mIU/L, or vitamin B12 below 200 pg/mL
addons.text: Show your TSH or vitamin B12 result to your doctor.
addons.why: Thyroid and vitamin levels can affect energy and mood.
